newsitem.title: UK: Weather dominates Europe grains sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Weather dominates Europe grains sentiment.

text.p: European grain traders focused on weather concerns as harvesting continued this week and with the market deprived of one of its main influences due to the absence of an EU export tender on Thursday,

Weather and quality concerns continued to dominate French domestic grain markets this week. Wheat business in France's main ports was at a standstill due to lack of fresh export news and uncertainty over quality.
Egypt is tendering over the weekend for 50,000 tonnes of French wheat but exporters doubt prices can be competitive against U.S. prices.
Rain in June and sporadic showers in July raised fears yields and quality may be hit in northern and eastern France. Rain is also slowing farmers' progress in some regions.
Sellers who feared they could not guarantee good milling wheat quality, bought back their positions in recent days, underpinning prices in Moselle, Rhin and Chalon/Modane areas.
But reports from the fields that the situation was not as bad as anticipated stopped the buying spree on Thursday.
Dealers said cooler temperatures in the north were expected to slow crop development, giving the grain plenty of time to mature and achieve satisfactory quality levels.
Reports from central France including the Beauce grain belt also suggested wheat and barley crops emerged largely unscathed from a prolonged spring drought.
Rouen barley was broadly unchanged due to the bleak export scene. Prices are unlikely to move unless the EU agrees more exports to non-EU countries.
Reports from the fields partially eased initial fears that a spring drought might have pushed up protein content, making a large part of the barley crop unfit for malting.
Demand from the starch industry pushed up old and new crop maize prices this week. There was also less concern from possible competition from a large feed wheat crop.
Currency was the main concern of the UK trade. "Currency is overriding everything," one trader in a big eastern co-operative said.

With a "reasonable amount" of old crop grain still around, the overall picture was depressing. But the failure of LIFFE futures prices to fall by as much as might have been expected when sterling leaped above 3.08 marks midweek, demonstrated there were buyers at current low sterling prices.

Harvest pressure reared its head on the futures market as farmers worked fast cutting barley in good weather at the start of the week. Farming sources reckoned sporadic showers on Thursday and Friday would do little to slow work.

Yields and quality of barley harvested so far have been highly variable, farmers and traders said. The co-operative trader expressed concern this harvest could produce "significantly more feed barley."
German grain markets are studying the effect of excessive rainfall on barley, rye and rapeseed but problems are too local and temporary to cause widespread nervousness, traders said.
Farmers were occupied with planning harvest schedules, rather than marketing, and consumers hoped for price falls amid volume pressure over the next two months.
Farmers feared delayed barley harvests might clash with the bulk of rapeseed harvesting and spring grain harvests and put a strain on storage capacity.
"There might be some sales pressure from the new crop at some stage which wouldn't be good for prices," one broker said.
But sellers hoped quality problems in France and grain losses from flooding in eastern Europe could open opportunities for German material.
Trades were thin on Friday, with some barley sought by the export trade and new crop feed wheat sold cif Oldenburg around 270 marks."

Spanish dealers said crops being harvested had been badly affected by storms and were expected to be low quality. However, ex-farm prices were not significantly higher in the week to July 24 as the bad weather had been taken into account in the previous week's prices.
Wheat harvests suffered from the rains, especially in Castilla Leon region where prices were quoted around 25,500 pesetas. Milling wheat was scarcely traded and dealers could not provide prices.

Durum wheat trade was active with many sales heading for the Italian market. Dealers said the Italian durum crop was very high quality and producers were keen to mix it with low quality Spanish durum wheat to balance the grain.
Durum wheat prices averaged 28,500 pesetas and ranged between 27,000 and 30,000.
The barley harvest was delayed by rain and quality has been badly affected by weather.
"When barley needed rain there was none and now it's at a stage when it doesn't need rain it has received too much," said one dealer.
But dealers said the Spanish maize crop had not been affected by rains. The maize harvest is due to start at the end of August.
Italian durum wheat prices rose in the week in line with increases in foreign markets.

The Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies (Ismea) noted millers were about to close down for the summer vacation but there is already demand for durum wheat with September delivery at higher prices than last year.
